Projectile motion describes the motion of an object that is thrown or launched into the air, subject only to acceleration due to gravity. Some examples of projectile motion include meteors entering Earth's atmosphere, fireworks, cannon balls, slash bullets, any ball and sports. The launched or thrown object is called a projectile and its path is called a trajectory. We consider 2D projectile motion which neglects the effects of air resistance. In projectile motion problems, the motions along perpendicular axes are independent and thus can be analyzed separately. The key to analyzing such problems is to break or separate the problem into two motions. A along the horizontal axis and B along the vertical axis. By convention, we call the horizontal axis the x-axis and the vertical axis the y-axis. We define a vector vector s to describe the total displacement while the vectors vector x and vector y are its component vectors along the respective axes. The magnitudes of these vectors are without arrows, s, x and y. Figure referenced in the course notes. Figure illustrates these vectors with a soccer player kicking a ball. Defining the positive direction as upward, the components of acceleration are a sub y equals minus g equals minus 9.81 meters per second squared minus 32.2 feet per second squared. A tennis player wins a match at Arthur Ashe Stadium and hits a ball into the stands at 30 meters per second and at an angle 45 degrees above the horizontal. On its way down, the ball is caught by a spectator 10 meters above the point where the ball was hit. A, calculate the time it takes the tennis ball to reach the spectator. B, what are the magnitude and direction of the ball's velocity at impact? Expand the drop down below to see the worked solution. The model. The ball is modeled as an ideal projectile. Air resistance is neglected, so the horizontal velocity remains constant and the vertical acceleration is downward. The launch point is taken as the origin with plus i hat horizontal and plus j hat upward. Because the spectator catches the ball above the launch point on the way down, the vertical position equation has two time solutions and the later solution is physically relevant. A, the catch time is found from the vertical position equation because the catch height is specified. Y equals Y sub zero plus V sub zero Y T minus 1 half G T squared. With the launch point as the origin and the catch point 10 meters above launch, the vertical equation becomes the quadratic equation 10 equals 21 T minus 1 half times 9.81 T squared. Zero equals 4.905 T squared minus 21 T plus 10. Solving this quadratic equation gives two possible times T equals 0.54 seconds or T equals 3.8 seconds. The later time corresponds to the ball descending into the stands, so the catch time is T equals 3.8 seconds. B, since the horizontal acceleration is zero, the horizontal velocity at impact remains equal to the initial horizontal velocity. V sub x equals 21 meters per second. The vertical velocity at impact comes from the vertical velocity equation. V sub Y equals V sub Y zero minus G T. Substituting the later catch time gives the downward vertical velocity at impact. V sub Y equals 21 meters per second minus 9.81 meters per second squared times 3.8 seconds equals negative 16 meters per second. Taking the magnitude of the velocity vector gives the impact speed V equals square root of V sub x to the power of 2 plus V sub Y to the power of 2 equals square root of 21 squared plus negative 16 squared meters per second equals 27 meters per second. Using the ratio of the vertical and horizontal velocity components gives the direction below the horizontal. Theta equals tan to the power of negative 1 of V sub Y over V sub X equals tan to the power of negative 1 of 16 over 21 equals 37 degrees. The conclusion. The ball reaches the spectator after 3.8 seconds. At impact, its speed is 27 meters per second and its direction is 37 degrees below the horizontal. The downward direction is consistent with the problem statement that the ball is caught on its way down and the speed is smaller than the launch speed because the ball is caught above its launch height. The problem. A golfer encounters two different situations on different holes. On the second hole, there are 120 meters from the green and want to hit the ball 90 meters and let it run onto the green. They angle the shot low to the ground at 30 degrees to the horizontal to let the ball roll after impact. On the fourth hole, there are 90 meters from the green and want to let the ball drop with the minimum amount of rolling after impact. Here, they angle the shot at 70 degrees to the horizontal to minimize rolling after impact. Both shots are hit and impacted on a level surface. A. What is the initial speed of the ball at the second hole? B. What is the initial speed of the ball at the fourth hole? C. Write the trajectory equation for both cases. D. Graph the trajectories. Expand the drop down below to see the worked solution. The model. Each golf shot is modeled as ideal projectile motion on level ground. Air resistance is neglected and the launch and impact heights are the same. The horizontal range can therefore be used to determine the initial speed for each launch angle. The trajectory equation is then written by eliminating time between the horizontal and vertical position equations. The math. For projectile motion that begins and ends at the same height, the horizontal range is related to the launch speed and launch angle by R equals V sub O to the power of 2 sine of 2 theta sub O over G. Solving the range equation for V sub O gives the launch speed needed for a specified range and angle. RG equals V sub O to the power of 2 sine of 2 theta sub O. RG over sine of 2 theta sub O equals V sub O to the power of 2. V sub O equals square root of RG over sine of 2 theta sub O. A. For the second hole, substituting R equals 90 meters and theta sub O equals 30 degrees gives the required launch speed V sub O equals square root of 90 meters times 9.81 meters per second squared over sine of 60 degrees equals 32 meters per second. B. For the fourth hole, substituting R equals 90 meters and theta sub O equals 70 degrees gives the required launch speed V sub O equals square root of 90 meters times 9.81 meters per second squared over sine of 140 degrees equals 37 meters per second. C. Eliminating time between the horizontal and vertical position equations for a projectile launched from the origin gives the trajectory equation Y of X equals X times tan theta sub O minus G over 2 times V sub O cos theta sub O squared times X squared. For the 30 degrees shot, substituting the launch angle and launch speed gives the low trajectory Y of X equals X tan 30 degrees minus 9.81 over 2 times 32 cosine 30 degrees squared X squared is approximately equal to 0.58X minus 0.0064X squared. For the 70 degree shot, substituting the launch angle and launch speed gives the high trajectory Y of X equals X tan 70 degrees minus 9.81 over 2 times 37 cosine 70 degrees squared X squared is approximately equal to 2.8X minus 0.031X squared. For part D, the graph is generated in the verification code by evaluating both trajectory equations from X equals 0 to X equals 90 meters. The conclusion. The second whole shot requires an initial speed of 32 meters per second at 30 degrees, while the fourth whole shot requires an initial speed of 37 meters per second at 70 degrees. The high angle trajectory is also much higher and steeper, which is why it lands with less horizontal motion available for rolling.

The problem. A tennis player wins a match at Arthur Ashe Stadium and hits a ball into the stands
at 30 meters per second and at an angle 45 degrees above the horizontal.
On its way down, the ball is caught by a spectator 10 meters above the point where the ball was hit.
A, calculate the time it takes the tennis ball to reach the spectator. B, what are the magnitude
and direction of the ball's velocity at impact? Expand the drop down below to see the worked solution.
The model. The ball is modeled as an ideal projectile. Air resistance is neglected,
so the horizontal velocity remains constant and the vertical acceleration is downward.
The launch point is taken as the origin with plus i hat horizontal and plus j hat upward.
Because the spectator catches the ball above the launch point on the way down,
the vertical position equation has two time solutions and the later solution is physically relevant.
A, the catch time is found
from the vertical position equation because the catch height is specified. Y equals Y sub zero plus
V sub zero Y T minus 1 half G T squared. With the launch point as the origin and the catch point
10 meters above launch, the vertical equation becomes the quadratic equation 10 equals 21 T minus
1 half times 9.81 T squared. Zero equals 4.905 T squared minus 21 T plus 10. Solving this quadratic
equation gives two possible times T equals 0.54 seconds or T equals 3.8 seconds.
The later time corresponds to the ball descending into the stands, so the catch time is T equals 3.8 seconds.
B, since the horizontal acceleration is zero, the horizontal velocity at impact remains equal to
the initial horizontal velocity. V sub x equals 21 meters per second. The vertical velocity at
impact comes from the vertical velocity equation. V sub Y equals V sub Y zero minus G T.
Substituting the later catch time gives the downward vertical velocity at impact.
V sub Y equals 21 meters per second minus 9.81 meters per second squared times 3.8 seconds equals
negative 16 meters per second. Taking the magnitude of the velocity vector gives the impact speed V
equals square root of V sub x to the power of 2 plus V sub Y to the power of 2 equals square
root of 21 squared plus negative 16 squared meters per second equals 27 meters per second.
Using the ratio of the vertical and horizontal velocity components gives the direction below
the horizontal. Theta equals tan to the power of negative 1 of V sub Y over V sub X equals tan to
the power of negative 1 of 16 over 21 equals 37 degrees. The conclusion. The ball reaches the
spectator after 3.8 seconds. At impact, its speed is 27 meters per second and its direction is 37
degrees below the horizontal. The downward direction is consistent with the problem statement that the
ball is caught on its way down and the speed is smaller than the launch speed because the ball is
caught above its launch height. The problem. A golfer encounters two different situations on different
holes. On the second hole, there are 120 meters from the green and want to hit the ball 90 meters
and let it run onto the green. They angle the shot low to the ground at 30 degrees to the
horizontal to let the ball roll after impact. On the fourth hole, there are 90 meters from the green
and want to let the ball drop with the minimum amount of rolling after impact. Here, they angle the
shot at 70 degrees to the horizontal to minimize rolling after impact. Both shots are hit and impacted
on a level surface. A. What is the initial speed of the ball at the second hole? B. What is the
initial speed of the ball at the fourth hole? C. Write the trajectory equation for both cases. D.
Graph the trajectories. Expand the drop down below to see the worked solution. The model.
Each golf shot is modeled as ideal projectile motion on level ground. Air resistance is neglected
and the launch and impact heights are the same. The horizontal range can therefore be used to
determine the initial speed for each launch angle. The trajectory equation is then written by
eliminating time between the horizontal and vertical position equations. The math. For projectile
motion that begins and ends at the same height, the horizontal range is related to the launch speed
and launch angle by R equals V sub O to the power of 2 sine of 2 theta sub O over G. Solving the
range equation for V sub O gives the launch speed needed for a specified range and angle. RG equals
V sub O to the power of 2 sine of 2 theta sub O. RG over sine of 2 theta sub O equals V sub O to the
power of 2. V sub O equals square root of RG over sine of 2 theta sub O. A. For the second hole,
substituting R equals 90 meters and theta sub O equals 30 degrees gives the required launch speed
V sub O equals square root of 90 meters times 9.81 meters per second squared over sine of 60
degrees equals 32 meters per second. B. For the fourth hole, substituting R equals 90 meters
and theta sub O equals 70 degrees gives the required launch speed V sub O equals square root of 90
meters times 9.81 meters per second squared over sine of 140 degrees equals 37 meters per second.
C. Eliminating time between the horizontal and vertical position equations for a projectile
launched from the origin gives the trajectory equation Y of X equals X times tan theta sub O minus G
over 2 times V sub O cos theta sub O squared times X squared. For the 30 degrees shot,
substituting the launch angle and launch speed gives the low trajectory Y of X equals X tan
30 degrees minus 9.81 over 2 times 32 cosine 30 degrees squared X squared is approximately equal
to 0.58X minus 0.0064X squared. For the 70 degree shot, substituting the launch angle and
launch speed gives the high trajectory Y of X equals X tan 70 degrees minus 9.81 over 2 times 37
cosine 70 degrees squared X squared is approximately equal to 2.8X minus 0.031X squared.
For part D, the graph is generated in the verification code by evaluating both trajectory equations
from X equals 0 to X equals 90 meters. The conclusion. The second whole shot requires an initial
speed of 32 meters per second at 30 degrees, while the fourth whole shot requires an initial speed
of 37 meters per second at 70 degrees. The high angle trajectory is also much higher and steeper,
which is why it lands with less horizontal motion available for rolling.
